prompt: Which description fits a single-replacement reaction?

choices.text: One element takes the place of another element in a compound
Two ionic compounds exchange ions, making two new compounds
choices.why: That describes a double-replacement reaction. In a single-replacement reaction, one of the reactants is an element.

choices.text: Two elements combine to make one new compound
choices.why: Nothing is replaced when two elements simply combine. A single-replacement reaction starts with an element and a compound.

choices.text: One compound breaks apart into two simpler substances
choices.why: Nothing is replaced when a compound simply breaks apart. A single replacement needs an element that takes another element's place in a compound.

explanation: In a single-replacement reaction, one element is substituted for another element in a compound. The products are a new element and a new compound.

prompt: Which equation represents a single-replacement reaction?

choices.why: Two compounds trade ions to make two new compounds, so this is a double-replacement reaction.
Both reactants are elements and the only product is a compound, so no element is replaced.
Elements form, but no element is a reactant, so nothing does any replacing. One compound just breaks apart.

explanation: A single-replacement equation has one element as a reactant and a different element as a product. Here nickel replaces copper in the compound, forming NiCl2 and copper metal.

prompt: Which equation represents a double-replacement reaction?

choices.why: An element (Mg) replaces another element (Fe) in a compound, so this is a single-replacement reaction.
There are two compounds as products, but only one reactant. A double-replacement reaction needs two compounds as reactants.
Two elements combine into one compound, so no parts are exchanged.

explanation: A double-replacement equation has two compounds as reactants and two different compounds as products. Here the cations trade partners: Ag^+ pairs with PO4^3− and Na^+ pairs with NO3^−.

prompt: In the reaction 2KI + Cl2 → 2KCl + I2, it is the negative ion in the compound that changes. What type of reaction is this?

choices.text: Single replacement, because the element chlorine replaces iodine in the compound
Double replacement, because the anion in the compound is exchanged
choices.why: Only one reactant is a compound; Cl2 is an element. A double replacement needs two compounds exchanging ions.

choices.text: Double replacement, because there are two reactants and two products
choices.why: Single-replacement reactions also have two reactants and two products. What matters is that one reactant and one product are elements.

choices.text: Not a replacement reaction, because only metals can replace other elements
choices.why: Halogens can replace one another too. An element replacing an anion is still a single-replacement reaction.

explanation: One reactant (Cl2) and one product (I2) are elements, the mark of a single-replacement reaction. Here the negatively charged ion changes from iodide to chloride.

prompt: Of the halogens fluorine, chlorine, bromine, and iodine, which one can replace each of the other three in their compounds?

choices.why: Iodine is lower in the halogen column than fluorine, so it can't replace fluorine.
Chlorine can't replace fluorine, which is above it in the halogen column.
Bromine can't replace fluorine or chlorine, which are both above it in the halogen column.

explanation: A halogen replaces the halogens below it in its column of the periodic table, but not those above it. Fluorine is at the top, so it can replace chlorine, bromine, and iodine.

prompt: Which proposed single-replacement reaction will occur?

choices.why: Bromine is below chlorine in the halogen column, so it can't replace chlorine.
Iodine is below bromine in the halogen column, so it can't replace bromine.
Iodine is below chlorine in the halogen column, so it can't replace chlorine.

explanation: A halogen replaces the halogens below it in its column of the periodic table, but not those above it. Bromine is above iodine, so it replaces the iodine in NaI.

prompt: Chlorine, Cl2, reacts with aluminum bromide, AlBr3, in a single-replacement reaction. Predict the products and balance the equation using the smallest whole-number coefficients. What is the coefficient of Cl2?
explanation: Chlorine replaces bromine, giving AlCl3 and Br2. One AlBr3 has 3 bromine atoms, an odd number that Br2 can't match, so double to 2AlBr3 and 2AlCl3; their 6 halogen atoms of each kind take 3Cl2 and release 3Br2: 3Cl2 + 2AlBr3 → 2AlCl3 + 3Br2.

prompt: How is an activity series used to predict whether a single-replacement reaction will occur?

choices.text: An element replaces elements listed below it, but not those listed above it
An element replaces elements listed above it, but not those listed below it
choices.why: This is backward. The element higher on the list does the replacing, just as a halogen replaces those below it.

choices.text: An element replaces only the one element listed directly below it
choices.why: An element can replace any element below it on the list, not just its nearest neighbor.

choices.text: Any element replaces any other; the list only shows how fast each reacts
choices.why: Elements will not replace elements above them, so some proposed single-replacement reactions don't occur at all.

explanation: An element on top replaces an element below it in a compound, but elements will not replace elements above them. Lithium, at the top of the series, can replace all the others; gold, at the bottom, replaces none.

prompt: The periodic table is enough to predict which halogen replaces which. Why is an activity series needed to predict which metal replaces which?

choices.text: A metal may or may not replace a nearby element, so the table shows no simple trend
Only a few elements form cations, so a short list is simpler than the table
choices.why: Many elements form cations. A list is needed because a metal may or may not replace an element near it on the periodic table.

choices.text: Metals replace the elements above them, the reverse of the halogen trend
choices.why: The activity series works like the halogen column: an element replaces the elements below it on the list.

choices.text: The activity series ranks metals by atomic mass, which the table doesn't show
choices.why: The series isn't in order of mass: barium, for example, is listed above much lighter sodium. It lists which elements replace which.

explanation: Replacing anions follows the halogens' positions on the periodic table, but replacing cations is not as straightforward: many elements form cations, and an element may replace another element nearby, or it may not. The activity series lists which elements replace which.

prompt: Which metal will react with hydrochloric acid, HCl(aq), by replacing the hydrogen and releasing H2 gas?

choices.why: Copper is below H2 in the activity series, so it can't replace hydrogen.
Silver is below H2 in the activity series, so it can't replace hydrogen.
Platinum is near the bottom of the activity series, well below H2, so it can't replace hydrogen.

explanation: H2 appears in the activity series, and metals above it replace hydrogen in compounds such as HCl. Magnesium is above H2, so Mg + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2 occurs.

prompt: Copper metal can replace an element in which of these compounds?

choices.why: H2 is above copper in the activity series, so copper can't replace hydrogen.
Lead is above copper in the activity series, so copper can't replace it.
Iron is above copper in the activity series, so copper can't replace it.

explanation: Copper replaces only elements below it in the activity series. Silver is below copper, so copper replaces it, forming copper(II) nitrate and silver metal.

prompt: A student predicts that a strip of copper placed in zinc sulfate solution, ZnSO4, will react to form CuSO4 and zinc metal. What is the correct prediction, and why?

choices.text: No reaction occurs, because copper is below zinc in the activity series
The reaction occurs, because copper is above zinc in the activity series
choices.why: Zinc is above copper in the activity series, not below it.

choices.text: The reaction occurs, because a free metal always replaces the metal in a compound
choices.why: An element replaces only the elements below it in the activity series, so some proposed reactions don't occur.

choices.text: No reaction occurs, because metals can replace hydrogen but not other metals
choices.why: Metals do replace other metals that are below them in the activity series. Copper just isn't above zinc.

explanation: Elements will not replace elements above them in the activity series. Zinc is above copper, so copper can't replace zinc, and no reaction is predicted.

prompt: Aluminum foil is placed in a solution of copper(II) chloride, CuCl2, and a single-replacement reaction occurs. Which equation correctly shows this reaction?

choices.why: The atoms balance, but AlCl2 isn't a proper formula: Al^3+ needs three Cl^− ions, so the product is AlCl3.
Copper and aluminum balance, but there are 6 chlorine atoms on the left and only 3 on the right.
This shows copper replacing aluminum, the reverse of what happens. Aluminum is above copper in the activity series, so aluminum replaces copper.

explanation: Aluminum is above copper in the activity series, so it replaces copper. Al^3+ pairs with three Cl^− to make AlCl3, and 2AlCl3 and 3CuCl2 both hold 6 chlorine atoms: 2Al + 3CuCl2 → 2AlCl3 + 3Cu.

prompt: A strip of magnesium is placed in a solution of silver nitrate, AgNO3. Predict the products of the single-replacement reaction and balance the equation using the smallest whole-number coefficients. What is the coefficient of silver, Ag?
explanation: Magnesium is above silver in the activity series, so it replaces silver. Mg^2+ pairs with two NO3^− ions to make Mg(NO3)2, so 2AgNO3 are needed, which release 2Ag: Mg + 2AgNO3 → Mg(NO3)2 + 2Ag.

prompt: A strip of zinc is placed in each of six separate solutions: FeSO4, MgSO4, NiSO4, AgNO3, Al(NO3)3, and Pb(NO3)2. In how many of the solutions will a single-replacement reaction occur?
explanation: Zinc replaces only elements below it in the activity series. Iron, nickel, silver, and lead are below zinc, but magnesium and aluminum are above it, so 4 reactions occur.

prompt: When predicting the products of a double-replacement reaction, you swap either the cations or the anions. Why not swap both?

choices.text: You would end up with the same substances you started with
The charges in the products would no longer balance
choices.why: Swapping both re-forms the original compounds, whose charges already balance. The problem is that nothing new forms.

choices.text: Each product would pair a cation with another cation
choices.why: Swapping both still pairs each cation with an anion, the same pairs you started with.

choices.text: The products would then always be insoluble
choices.why: Solubility doesn't depend on how you swap. Swapping both simply gives back the reactants.

explanation: Swapping the cations and swapping the anions are two equivalent ways of describing the same exchange. Doing both undoes the exchange and gives back the original compounds.

prompt: What are the products of the double-replacement reaction between nickel(II) nitrate, Ni(NO3)2, and potassium phosphate, K3PO4?

choices.why: Ni^2+ and PO4^3− don't balance one to one. It takes three Ni^2+ (6+) to balance two PO4^3− (6−).
These formulas keep the subscripts from the reactants. Product subscripts must be worked out from the charges of the new ion pairs.
The numbers are reversed: two Ni^2+ give 4+, but three PO4^3− give 9−. It takes three Ni^2+ and two PO4^3−.

explanation: Exchanging partners pairs Ni^2+ with PO4^3− and K^+ with NO3^−. Balancing the charges gives Ni3(PO4)2 (6+ and 6−) and KNO3 (1+ and 1−).

prompt: What is a precipitation reaction?

choices.text: A double-replacement reaction in which one product is an insoluble solid
A double-replacement reaction in which one product is a gas
choices.why: A precipitate is a solid that doesn't dissolve, not a gas.

choices.text: A single-replacement reaction in which one metal replaces another
choices.why: A precipitation reaction happens between two dissolved ionic compounds that exchange ions, so it is a double-replacement reaction.

choices.text: A process in which a solid ionic compound dissolves in water
choices.why: That is dissolving. In a precipitation reaction, a new compound forms that does not dissolve and falls out of solution.

explanation: A precipitation reaction occurs when two dissolved ionic compounds form a new ionic compound that does not dissolve. It falls out of solution as a solid precipitate, and its formation is what drives the reaction.

prompt: Solutions of two soluble ionic compounds are mixed. According to the solubility rules, both possible double-replacement products are also soluble. What do you predict?

choices.text: No reaction occurs, because no precipitate forms
A reaction occurs, and both products are labeled (aq)
choices.why: Without an insoluble product, nothing drives the reaction. If everything is soluble, no reaction is expected.

choices.text: A reaction occurs, and both products settle out as solids
choices.why: Soluble compounds stay dissolved. Only an insoluble product falls out of solution as a precipitate.
A single-replacement reaction needs an element as a reactant, and both reactants here are compounds.

explanation: The formation of a solid precipitate is the driving force for this kind of double-replacement reaction. If the reactants and all the possible products are soluble, no reaction is expected.

prompt: According to the solubility rules, compounds of which anion are soluble with no exceptions?

choices.why: Most chlorides are soluble, but a few cations are exceptions.
Most sulfates are soluble, but a few cations are exceptions.
Carbonates are generally insoluble; only the carbonates of a few cations dissolve.

explanation: All compounds of NO3^− (nitrate) and C2H3O2^− (acetate) are soluble, with no exceptions. Chlorides and sulfates are generally soluble but have exceptions, and carbonates are generally insoluble.

prompt: Most compounds of the sulfate ion, SO4^2−, are soluble. Which cation is an exception, forming an insoluble sulfate?

choices.why: All sodium compounds are soluble, so Na2SO4 dissolves.
Mg^2+ is not one of the exceptions to the sulfate rule, so MgSO4 is soluble.
Al^3+ is not one of the exceptions to the sulfate rule, so Al2(SO4)3 is soluble.

explanation: Pb^2+ is one of the few cations whose sulfate does not dissolve, so PbSO4 is insoluble. The sulfates of Na^+, Mg^2+, and Al^3+ are soluble.

prompt: According to the solubility rules, which compound is insoluble in water?

choices.why: Silver is an exception only for Cl^−, Br^−, and I^− compounds. Silver nitrate dissolves.
Iodides are generally soluble, and Mg^2+ is not one of the exceptions.
Phosphates are generally insoluble, but compounds of NH4^+ are an exception.

explanation: Compounds of I^− are generally soluble, but Ag^+ is one of the exceptions, so AgI is insoluble.

prompt: According to the solubility rules, how many of these compounds are insoluble in water: MgBr2, Fe(OH)3, Na3PO4, SrSO4, Ba(OH)2, ZnCO3?
explanation: Fe(OH)3 (hydroxides are generally insoluble), SrSO4 (Sr^2+ is an exception for sulfates), and ZnCO3 (carbonates are generally insoluble) don't dissolve. MgBr2 (bromides are generally soluble), Na3PO4 (sodium compounds are always soluble), and Ba(OH)2 (Ba^2+ is an exception for hydroxides) do, so 3 are insoluble.

prompt: Solutions of sodium carbonate, Na2CO3, and calcium nitrate, Ca(NO3)2, are mixed. What precipitate forms, if any?

choices.why: All sodium compounds are soluble, so NaNO3 stays dissolved.
Ca^2+ and CO3^2− balance one to one, so the formula is CaCO3.
Carbonates are generally insoluble, and Ca^2+ is not one of the exceptions, so CaCO3 precipitates.

explanation: Exchanging ions gives CaCO3 and NaNO3. NaNO3 is soluble, but carbonates are insoluble unless the cation is Li^+, Na^+, K^+, Rb^+, Cs^+, or NH4^+, so CaCO3 precipitates.

prompt: Which pair of solutions will form a precipitate when mixed?

choices.why: The possible products are KNO3 and (NH4)2CO3. Ammonium compounds are an exception to the carbonate rule, so both are soluble.
The possible products, NaNO3 and ZnBr2, are both soluble; Zn^2+ isn't an exception for bromides.
The possible products are Pb(C2H3O2)2 and KNO3. Acetates are always soluble, and KNO3 is a potassium compound, so both dissolve.

explanation: Exchanging ions in CuSO4 and KOH gives Cu(OH)2 and K2SO4. Hydroxides are generally insoluble and Cu^2+ isn't an exception, so Cu(OH)2 precipitates.

prompt: A student predicts that mixing solutions of Na2SO4 and Zn(NO3)2 will produce a precipitate of ZnSO4. Is the student right?

choices.text: No; both possible products, ZnSO4 and NaNO3, are soluble
Yes; sulfates are generally insoluble, so ZnSO4 precipitates
choices.why: It's the reverse: sulfates are generally soluble, and Zn^2+ is not one of the exceptions.

choices.text: No; NaNO3 is the product that precipitates instead
choices.why: All sodium compounds are soluble, so NaNO3 stays dissolved.

choices.text: Yes; mixing two ionic solutions always produces a precipitate
choices.why: Mixing two ionic solutions doesn't always give a precipitate. Here neither possible product is insoluble.

explanation: Exchanging ions gives ZnSO4 and NaNO3. Sulfates are generally soluble and Zn^2+ is not an exception, and all sodium compounds are soluble, so both stay dissolved and no precipitate forms.

prompt: Solutions of lead(II) nitrate and potassium iodide react in a double-replacement reaction. Which equation shows the correct phase labels?

choices.why: These labels are swapped. KNO3 is a potassium compound, so it is soluble; PbI2 is the insoluble product.
PbI2 isn't soluble: Pb^2+ is one of the exceptions for iodides, so PbI2 forms as a solid precipitate.
The reactants are dissolved, and both are soluble (a nitrate and a potassium compound), so they are labeled (aq).

explanation: Soluble compounds get the (aq) label and insoluble ones get (s). Pb(NO3)2, KI, and KNO3 are soluble, but Pb^2+ is an exception for iodides, so PbI2 is labeled (s).

prompt: A waste solution contains dissolved barium nitrate, Ba(NO3)2. Which solution could be added to remove the barium ions as a precipitate?

choices.why: Ba^2+ is an exception to the hydroxide rule, so Ba(OH)2 is soluble and no precipitate forms.
Ba^2+ is not an exception for chlorides, so BaCl2 is soluble and no precipitate forms.
Acetates are always soluble, so barium acetate would stay dissolved.

explanation: Exchanging ions with Na2SO4 gives BaSO4 and NaNO3. Ba^2+ is one of the exceptions to the sulfate rule, so BaSO4 is insoluble and precipitates, taking the barium ions out of solution.

prompt: Solutions of iron(III) sulfate, Fe2(SO4)3, and sodium hydroxide, NaOH, undergo a double-replacement reaction. Predict the products and balance the equation using the smallest whole-number coefficients. What is the coefficient of NaOH?
explanation: The products are Fe(OH)3 (Fe^3+ needs three OH^−) and Na2SO4. Two iron atoms need 2Fe(OH)3, which takes 6 OH^−, so 6NaOH; the 6 Na^+ then make 3Na2SO4: Fe2(SO4)3 + 6NaOH → 2Fe(OH)3 + 3Na2SO4.

prompt: Solutions of aluminum chloride, AlCl3, and silver nitrate, AgNO3, undergo a double-replacement reaction. Predict the products and balance the equation using the smallest whole-number coefficients. What is the sum of all the coefficients, counting any coefficient of 1?
explanation: The products are AgCl and Al(NO3)3. The three Cl^− in one AlCl3 need 3AgNO3 and form 3AgCl, leaving one Al(NO3)3: AlCl3 + 3AgNO3 → 3AgCl + Al(NO3)3. The coefficients 1 + 3 + 3 + 1 add up to 8.
